title: Swift Fundamentals for Kotlin Developers
scopeHtml: Scope: Syntax tour vs Kotlin, let/var, type inference, optionals and unwrapping, control flow, functions and argument labels, closures, strings, access control, tuples.

notes.title: Baseline and the big picture
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android you write Kotlin in Android Studio, build with Gradle, and target an minSdk. In iOS you write Swift in Xcode, build with the Xcode build system (and Swift Package Manager for dependencies), and target a minimum iOS version.

Baseline used in all these notes. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 as the minimum deployment target, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials. Modern APIs are the default: @Observable, NavigationStack, SwiftData, async/await, actors, Swift Testing (import Testing, @Test, #expect), async URLSession, Swift Package Manager. Legacy forms (ObservableObject, NavigationView, Core Data, Combine, XCTest, completion handlers) appear only under a "you will meet this in old codebases" label. Anything new in iOS 18/26 is marked verify.

Swift and Kotlin are close cousins. Both are statically typed, compiled (Swift to native machine code through LLVM, Kotlin to JVM bytecode or native), type-inferred, null-safe, with first-class functions, generics, extensions and protocol/interface-based design. The differences that bite are: Swift has value types as the default (struct, enum), no garbage collector (ARC instead), argument labels at call sites, no checked exceptions but explicit try, and optionals are a real enum rather than a nullable flag.

Android iOS
Kotlin Swift
Gradle / Maven Swift Package Manager (SPM), Xcode build system
Android Studio Xcode
minSdk Deployment target
JVM + GC Native code + ARC
.kt file in a package .swift file in a module (target)
build.gradle Package.swift / .xcodeproj build settings

Real industry examples. Airbnb, Uber and Lyft have large Swift codebases; Uber famously rewrote its rider app in Swift (the "RIBs" architecture exists in both Swift and Kotlin). Apple's own frameworks (SwiftUI, Swift Charts, SwiftData) are Swift-first.

Everyday analogy. Moving from Kotlin to Swift is like moving from driving an automatic to driving a manual in another country: the same road rules and destination, but the controls sit in slightly different places and a few habits (like checking the other side) must change.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Swift runs on a VM or has a garbage collector. It does neither; memory is managed by ARC (see 02_L2).
  • Assuming Swift is "Kotlin with different keywords". The value-type default and argument labels change design decisions.
  • Forgetting that a Swift file does not declare a package; the unit of encapsulation is the module.

notes.title: let, var and type inference
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin has val (read-only reference) and var (mutable). Swift has let (constant) and var (variable). They map one to one, but Swift's let on a struct makes the whole value immutable, which val does not do for a Kotlin object's contents.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
let name = "Asha"          // constant, inferred String
var count = 0              // mutable, inferred Int
count += 1
let ratio: Double = 3      // explicit annotation; 3 is a literal that adapts
// name = "Ravi"           // compile error: cannot assign to 'let'
val name = "Asha"          // read-only, inferred String
var count = 0              // mutable, inferred Int
count += 1
val ratio: Double = 3.0    // Kotlin does not widen an Int literal to Double
// name = "Ravi"           // compile error: val cannot be reassigned

How inference works. Swift infers a type from the right side of the assignment. Integer literals default to Int (64-bit on all current Apple platforms), float literals to Double, strings to String, and a literal can adapt to the annotated type (let ratio: Double = 3 is legal in Swift, an error in Kotlin). There is no implicit numeric conversion between typed values: Int plus Double does not compile, you write Double(count) + ratio. Kotlin is the same (no implicit widening), except for literals.

let and value types. let freezes a struct completely:

struct Point { var x: Int; var y: Int }
let p = Point(x: 1, y: 2)
// p.x = 5          // error: p is a let constant, so its stored properties are immutable
var q = p           // q is an independent copy
q.x = 5             // fine

With a class, let c = Counter() only fixes the reference; c.value = 5 still works. This is the same as Kotlin val with a mutable object.

Compiler behaviour. Prefer let everywhere; the compiler can optimise constants and the Swift style guides (and SwiftLint's prefer_let-style warnings) flag a var that is never mutated. Very long expressions with many literals and operators can make type-checking slow ("the compiler is unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time"), a real production build-time issue; the fix is to split the expression and annotate intermediate types.

Real industry examples. Airbnb's Swift style guide and Apple's API Design Guidelines both say to default to let. SwiftLint ships rules that warn on never-mutated var.

Everyday analogy. let is a name written in permanent marker on a locker; var is the same locker with a whiteboard label. For a struct, the marker covers everything inside the locker, not just the label.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing let on a class instance makes the object immutable. It fixes only the reference.
  • Expecting Int and Double to mix like in a scripting language. They do not.
  • Thinking Int is 32-bit. On 64-bit Apple platforms Int is 64-bit (Int32 exists separately).

notes.title: Optionals versus Kotlin nullability
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Kotlin String? is a compiler-tracked nullable type with no wrapper at runtime. In Swift String? is sugar for Optional<String>, a real generic enum with two cases, .none and .some(Wrapped). Same intent, different representation.

// Conceptually, the standard library defines:
// enum Optional<Wrapped> { case none; case some(Wrapped) }
let a: String? = "hi"            // .some("hi")
let b: String? = nil             // .none

Because Optional is an enum, you can switch on it, map over it, and nest it (Int??), which Kotlin's flat nullability cannot express. For types like class references, the compiler stores .none as the null pointer (no extra byte); for Int? it adds a tag byte, so MemoryLayout<Int?>.size is 9 while MemoryLayout<Int>.size is 8 (verify with MemoryLayout).

The operators map like this:

Kotlin Swift Meaning
x?.foo() x?.foo() optional chaining, result is optional
x ?: d x ?? d default if nil
x!! x! force unwrap, crash if nil
if (x != null) smart cast if let x { } bind a non-optional name
x?.let { } if let x { } or x.map { } run only if present
lateinit var var x: T! (implicitly unwrapped) trust it will be set
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func greet(_ user: User?) -> String {
    let name = user?.profile?.displayName ?? "Guest"   // chaining + default
    return "Hello, \(name)"
}
fun greet(user: User?): String {
    val name = user?.profile?.displayName ?: "Guest"
    return "Hello, $name"
}

Key difference: smart casts. Kotlin smart-casts x after if (x != null). Swift does not narrow the same variable; you rebind with if let x (shorthand since Swift 5.7 for if let x = x) or guard let. This is why Swift code is full of if let.

Implicitly unwrapped optionals (T!). Declared as var label: UILabel!. It behaves as optional but auto-unwraps on use and crashes if nil. It exists for two-phase initialisation, historically @IBOutlets. In modern SwiftUI code you almost never need it.

Production incident pattern. Fatal error: Unexpectedly found nil while unwrapping an Optional value is the top Swift crash signature (EXC_BAD_INSTRUCTION / SIGILL in the crash report). Typical causes: ! on a decoded JSON field, an IBOutlet accessed before the view loaded, URL(string:)! with an unescaped string at runtime.

Real industry examples. Alamofire and Kingfisher return optionals/Results rather than force unwrapping; Firebase's Swift SDK returns Optional errors in completion handlers. Teams like Airbnb and Spotify ban ! in their lint config except in tests.

Everyday analogy. An Optional is a gift box that may be empty. Kotlin lets you look through the wrapper paper ("the value is either a thing or nothing"); Swift makes you open the box (if let) before you use the contents.

Common interview traps.

  • Using ! to "make the compiler quiet". It converts a compile-time safety net into a crash.
  • Saying Optional is a nullable pointer. It is an enum; Int? is not a pointer.
  • Confusing ?? (default) with ?. (chaining), and forgetting chaining returns an optional.
  • Expecting Kotlin-style smart casts after a nil check.

notes.title: Unwrapping: if let, guard let, optional binding
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin uses ?.let { }, early return after a null check with a smart cast, or requireNotNull. Swift's idiom is if let for a scoped branch and guard let for an early exit that keeps the name in scope afterward.

func load(id: String?) {
    // 1. if let: name exists only inside the braces
    if let id {                       // Swift 5.7 shorthand for `if let id = id`
        print("loading \(id)")
    }

    // 2. multiple conditions, comma means AND
    if let id, !id.isEmpty, let n = Int(id), n > 0 {
        print("positive int \(n)")
    }

    // 3. guard let: name exists for the rest of the function
    guard let id else { return }
    print(id.count)
}

Other unwrapping tools.

  • ?? with a default, including with throw-style fallbacks using a closure: value ?? computeDefault() (the right side is lazily evaluated, an autoclosure).
  • map / flatMap on Optional: let len = name.map(\.count).
  • switch with case .some(let v) or case let v?.
  • try? converts a throwing call to an optional; try! crashes on error.
  • while let loops until nil (iterators).
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
let ids = ["1", "x", "3"]
let numbers = ids.compactMap { Int($0) }        // [1, 3]; drops nils
val ids = listOf("1", "x", "3")
val numbers = ids.mapNotNull { it.toIntOrNull() }   // [1, 3]

Real industry examples. Nearly every decoded-model layer (Codable) produces optionals for missing JSON keys; apps like Instagram-style feeds use compactMap to drop invalid items rather than crash. SwiftUI previews and tests often use try XCTUnwrap (XCTest) or try #require(...) (Swift Testing) to unwrap or fail the test.

Everyday analogy. if let is checking the mailbox: only if a letter is there do you step inside the house with it. guard let is a bouncer: no letter, no entry, and anyone past the door is guaranteed to have one.

Common interview traps.

  • Shadowing confusion: if let x = x creates a new x; mutating it does not change the original optional.
  • Using try? and losing the error, which hides real failures.
  • Chaining ! in several places "just to compile".
  • Assuming if let a = x, let b = y is OR; the comma is AND.

notes.title: guard and early exit
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Kotlin you write val a = x ?: return or if (x == null) return followed by smart-cast use. Swift's guard makes the early-exit pattern explicit and the compiler enforces that the else block leaves the scope.

func upload(user: User?, data: Data?) async throws {
    guard let user else { throw UploadError.notSignedIn }
    guard let data, !data.isEmpty else { throw UploadError.emptyPayload }
    guard user.isActive else { return }       // exits, no value needed in Void func

    try await send(data, for: user)           // happy path flat, not nested
}
Languages: Kotlin
suspend fun upload(user: User?, data: ByteArray?) {
    val u = user ?: throw UploadError.NotSignedIn
    val d = data?.takeIf { it.isNotEmpty() } ?: throw UploadError.EmptyPayload
    if (!u.isActive) return
    send(d, u)
}

Rules. The else body must exit: return, throw, break, continue or call a Never-returning function such as fatalError. Variables bound by guard let are visible in the enclosing scope after the statement, which is the main difference from if let.

Why it matters. It avoids the "pyramid of doom" of nested if let. Style guides at Apple, Airbnb and Ray Wenderlich/Kodeco recommend guard for preconditions and if let for optional branches that are one of several paths.

Production note. guard combined with defer is a common resource pattern: defer runs when the scope exits by any path, including the guard's early return.

func readFile(at url: URL) throws -> Data {
    let handle = try FileHandle(forReadingFrom: url)
    defer { try? handle.close() }              // always runs on exit
    guard let data = try handle.readToEnd() else { return Data() }
    return data
}

Everyday analogy. guard is a security gate at the start of a corridor: failing the checks sends you straight out. Everyone inside the corridor is guaranteed to have passed.

Common interview traps.

  • Writing a guard whose else does not exit; it is a compile error.
  • Thinking guard let scopes the name to the else block. It is the opposite: it leaks into the rest of the function.
  • Using guard for a case where both branches do real work; if/else is clearer.

notes.title: Control flow and switch
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin has if as expression, when, for, while. Swift has if/switch (both usable as expressions since Swift 5.9), for-in, while, repeat-while.

let score = 82
let grade = switch score {          // switch expression, Swift 5.9+
case 90...: "A"
case 80..<90: "B"
case ..<80: "C"
default: "?"
}

let label = if score >= 50 { "pass" } else { "fail" }   // if expression

for i in 0..<3 { print(i) }                 // half-open range
for (index, item) in ["a", "b"].enumerated() { print(index, item) }
outer: for x in 1...3 { for y in 1...3 { if x * y == 4 { break outer } } }
Languages: Kotlin
val grade = when {
    score >= 90 -> "A"
    score in 80..89 -> "B"
    else -> "C"
}
for (i in 0 until 3) println(i)
for ((index, item) in listOf("a", "b").withIndex()) println("$index $item")

Differences to remember.

  • switch must be exhaustive and cases do not fall through (no break needed). Use fallthrough to opt in.
  • Each case body needs at least one statement.
  • Patterns are rich: ranges, tuples, where clauses, enum payload binding (covered fully in 04_L4).
  • Swift has no C-style for (i = 0; ...) loop and no ++/--.
  • stride(from:to:by:) replaces stepping loops (Kotlin step).
switch (point.x, point.y) {
case (0, 0): print("origin")
case (let x, 0): print("on x axis at \(x)")
case let (x, y) where x == y: print("diagonal")
default: print("elsewhere")
}

Everyday analogy. switch is a sorting machine at a post office that must have a bin for every possible parcel; if you forget a bin the machine will not start (compile error).

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting C-style fallthrough or adding needless break.
  • Forgetting default on a non-enum switch; the compiler requires exhaustiveness.
  • Assuming ... and ..< ranges behave the same as Kotlin .. and until; 1...3 is inclusive, 1..<3 excludes 3.

notes.title: Functions and argument labels
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin has positional parameters with optional named arguments (foo(x = 1)). Swift has argument labels baked into the function's name: move(from:to:). Every parameter has an external label (what the caller writes) and an internal name (used in the body), and the labels are part of the signature.

func move(from start: Int, to end: Int) -> Int { end - start }   // call: move(from: 2, to: 9)
func area(_ w: Double, _ h: Double) -> Double { w * h }           // _ drops the label: area(2, 3)
func greet(name: String, punctuation: String = "!") -> String {   // default value
    "Hi \(name)\(punctuation)"
}
greet(name: "Asha")            // default used
greet(name: "Asha", punctuation: "?")
Languages: Kotlin
fun move(from: Int, to: Int): Int = to - from        // call: move(2, 9) or move(from = 2, to = 9)
fun area(w: Double, h: Double) = w * h
fun greet(name: String, punctuation: String = "!") = "Hi $name$punctuation"

Why labels exist. Swift's API Design Guidelines want call sites to read like English: array.insert(x, at: 3), view.addSubview(label), UIColor(red:green:blue:alpha:). Methods are named including their labels in documentation: insert(_:at:). Overloads can differ only by labels, so foo(a:) and foo(b:) are different functions.

More parameter forms.

  • Variadic: func sum(_ n: Int...) where n is [Int].
  • inout: func bump(_ x: inout Int) { x += 1 }, called as bump(&v); copy-in copy-out semantics.
  • Multiple returns via tuples; implicit return for single-expression bodies.
  • async throws markers sit before the arrow: func load() async throws -> Data.
  • Functions are first-class: let f: (Int, Int) -> Int = (+).
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func divide(_ a: Int, by b: Int) throws -> (quotient: Int, remainder: Int) {
    guard b != 0 else { throw MathError.divideByZero }
    return (a / b, a % b)
}
let result = try divide(7, by: 2)        // result.quotient, result.remainder
fun divide(a: Int, b: Int): Pair<Int, Int> {
    require(b != 0) { "divide by zero" }
    return a / b to a % b
}

Real industry examples. All of Apple's frameworks and popular libraries (Alamofire's AF.request(_:method:parameters:), Kingfisher's imageView.kf.setImage(with:)) follow label conventions. Getting a label wrong is the most common Swift compile error for newcomers.

Everyday analogy. Labels are like the fields on a paper form: "From ___ To ___". You do not need to remember the order, the form tells you.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling move(2, 9) and being surprised it fails: labels are mandatory unless _.
  • Confusing internal and external names in the declaration order (label name: Type).
  • Thinking Kotlin named arguments and Swift labels are the same: Kotlin's are optional at call sites, Swift's are required.

notes.title: Closures, trailing closure syntax and @escaping
notes.html:
Android equivalent. A Kotlin lambda { x -> x + 1 } is a Swift closure { x in x + 1 }. Both can be passed as the last argument outside the parentheses. Swift closures capture variables by reference like Kotlin lambdas, but Swift requires you to think about whether a closure outlives the function (@escaping).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
let nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
let doubled = nums.map { $0 * 2 }                     // $0 shorthand
let evens = nums.filter { $0 % 2 == 0 }
let total = nums.reduce(0) { acc, n in acc + n }
let sorted = nums.sorted { a, b in a > b }
val nums = listOf(1, 2, 3, 4)
val doubled = nums.map { it * 2 }                      // 'it'
val evens = nums.filter { it % 2 == 0 }
val total = nums.fold(0) { acc, n -> acc + n }
val sorted = nums.sortedByDescending { it }

Syntax forms. Full: { (a: Int, b: Int) -> Int in a + b }. Inferred: { a, b in a + b }. Shorthand: { $0 + $1 }. Operator reference: reduce(0, +). Key-path as function: names.map(\.count). Trailing closure: if the last parameter is a closure, write f(x) { ... }; with multiple (Swift 5.3+) you write f { } onError: { } with labels on all but the first.

Non-escaping vs @escaping. By default a closure parameter is non-escaping: it may only be called during the function and cannot be stored. The compiler can then keep it on the stack and skip reference counting. If the closure is stored or called later (a completion handler, a Task, a stored property) you must mark it @escaping. This is a hard compile error otherwise, and there is no Kotlin equivalent (Kotlin has inline/noinline/crossinline for a different reason).

final class Loader {
    private var handlers: [() -> Void] = []
    func onReady(_ work: @escaping () -> Void) { handlers.append(work) }   // stored
    func run(_ work: () -> Void) { work() }                                // not stored
}

Capture lists. Closures capture surrounding variables strongly by default. A capture list [weak self], [unowned self] or [value] in square brackets controls this:

class Screen {
    var title = "Home"
    var onTap: (() -> Void)?
    func setup() {
        onTap = { [weak self] in          // avoids a retain cycle
            guard let self else { return }
            print(self.title)
        }
        var n = 0
        let snapshot = { [n] in n }        // captures value 0 at creation, not the variable
        n = 5
        print(snapshot())                   // 0
    }
}

Capture of self in an escaping closure inside a class requires an explicit self. (or [self] in the list) to make the capture visible. The full memory story is in 02_L2. In Swift 6 a closure that crosses concurrency domains must be @Sendable (see the concurrency notes).

Real industry examples. Nearly all pre-async networking code (Alamofire completion handlers, URLSession.dataTask, Firebase callbacks) is @escaping. SwiftUI's Button("Go") { ... } and ForEach(items) { item in ... } use trailing closures; result builders (@ViewBuilder) are closures with special syntax.

Everyday analogy. A non-escaping closure is a note you hand to a waiter who reads it at your table and gives it back. An escaping closure is a note you leave with the kitchen to act on later, so you must make sure it still makes sense when they read it.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting @escaping on a stored completion and reading the compile error as a bug in the compiler.
  • Using [weak self] everywhere by reflex; non-escaping closures and short-lived Tasks do not need it.
  • Thinking [n] captures a reference; it captures a copy at creation time.
  • Writing $0 in nested closures and confusing which closure it belongs to.

notes.title: Strings and string interpolation
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin String is a UTF-16 sequence indexed by Int. Swift String is a collection of extended grapheme clusters (Character), stored as UTF-8 internally since Swift 5. You cannot index by integer, because the Nth character is not at a fixed byte offset.

let s = "Café 👨‍👩‍👧"
s.count                                  // counts Characters (family emoji = 1)
s.utf8.count                             // bytes
let i = s.index(s.startIndex, offsetBy: 2)
s[i]                                     // "f"
let first = s.first                       // Character?
let word = s.prefix(4)                    // Substring, shares storage
let copy = String(word)                   // make an independent String
"Hello, \(s.count) chars"                 // interpolation
let multi = """
    Line one
      indented relative
    """                                    // multiline literal; closing quotes set indentation
let raw = #"C:\path\n stays literal"#     // raw string
Languages: Kotlin
val s = "Café"
s.length                  // UTF-16 code units
s[2]                       // 'f' by Int index
val word = s.take(4)
"Hello, ${s.length} chars"
val multi = """
    Line one
""".trimIndent()

Value semantics and COW. String is a struct with copy-on-write storage (details in 02_L2). Small strings up to 15 UTF-8 bytes are stored inline in the 16-byte struct with no heap allocation (a "small string" optimisation on 64-bit; verify exact size). Substring is a view into the original string's storage and keeps the whole parent string alive, a known memory-retention trap if you store substrings long term.

Handy API. hasPrefix, contains, split(separator:), replacingOccurrences(of:with:) (Foundation), trimmingCharacters(in:), lowercased(). Foundation's String bridging (NSString) adds locale-aware compare: localizedCompare, localizedCaseInsensitiveContains. Use String(localized:) for localisation (iOS 15+).

Production note. Comparing strings with == is canonical equivalence: "é" (one scalar) equals "e\u{301}" (two scalars). Sorting user-visible names should use localizedStandardCompare, as Finder does.

Real industry examples. Messaging apps (WhatsApp-style) measure emoji and flags by Character, not UTF-16 length, to avoid cutting a flag in half. Swift Regex (import RegexBuilder, Swift 5.7+) replaces many NSRegularExpression uses.

Everyday analogy. A Swift string is a necklace of beads where beads differ in width (a plain letter, a multi-part emoji). To reach bead number 5 you must walk along the string; you cannot jump by arithmetic.

Common interview traps.

  • Trying s[2]; it does not compile. Use index(_:offsetBy:) or convert to Array(s).
  • Assuming count is O(1). It is O(n) because it must walk grapheme clusters.
  • Holding on to a Substring and wondering why a big string never frees.
  • Comparing with == for sorting to humans instead of locale-aware compare.

notes.title: Tuples and ranges
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin has Pair/Triple and destructuring, plus IntRange. Swift tuples are anonymous structural types written (Int, String) with optional element names, usable as multiple return values, and Swift has Range, ClosedRange and partial ranges as first-class types.

let http = (code: 404, message: "Not Found")
http.code; http.0                         // named and positional access
let (code, message) = http                // destructuring
let (min, max) = nums.min().flatMap { m in nums.max().map { (m, $0) } } ?? (0, 0)

func bounds(of xs: [Int]) -> (low: Int, high: Int)? {
    guard let lo = xs.min(), let hi = xs.max() else { return nil }
    return (lo, hi)
}
Languages: Kotlin
val http = 404 to "Not Found"            // Pair<Int, String>, no names
val (code, message) = http
fun bounds(xs: List<Int>): Pair<Int, Int>? {
    val lo = xs.minOrNull() ?: return null
    return lo to xs.max()
}

Limits. Tuples cannot conform to protocols (they are not nominal types) and cannot be Equatable automatically beyond == on tuples up to arity 6 by the standard library. Beyond two or three values, use a struct. Using a tuple as a dictionary key is impossible because tuples are not Hashable.

Ranges. 1...5 (ClosedRange), 1..<5 (Range), ...5, 5..., ..<5 (partial). They slice collections: arr[1...3] returns an ArraySlice (a view that shares storage and keeps the original indices, another memory-retention trap, identical in spirit to Substring). stride(from: 0, to: 10, by: 2) steps.

Real industry examples. URLSession returns a (Data, URLResponse) tuple from data(for:); Dictionary.enumerated() and zip produce tuples. Codebases at scale usually promote tuples to small structs once more than one caller uses them.

Everyday analogy. A tuple is a sticky note with two or three scribbles; useful for a moment. When the note gets passed around the office, you print a proper form (a struct).

Common interview traps.

  • Using a tuple as a long-lived model type; it cannot adopt protocols.
  • Slicing an array and indexing the slice from 0; slices keep original indices.
  • Confusing 0...n with 0..<n in for loops and off-by-one crashing on arr[n].

notes.title: Access control levels
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin has public (default), internal (module), protected, private. Swift's default is internal (module) and it has five (six since Swift 5.9) levels, with fileprivate and open having no direct Kotlin twin.

Swift Visible to Kotlin analogue
private enclosing declaration and its same-file extensions private
fileprivate whole source file (no equivalent; closest is top-level private in a file)
internal (default) whole module internal (but Kotlin default is public)
package all modules in the same Swift package (Swift 5.9+) no equivalent
public other modules, but cannot subclass or override outside the module public final
open other modules and subclass/override allowed (classes and members only) public open 
public struct Money {                    // visible to other modules
    public let amount: Decimal
    private(set) public var currency: String   // readable publicly, settable only inside
    public init(amount: Decimal, currency: String) { self.amount = amount; self.currency = currency }
}
open class BaseViewController: UIViewController {}   // framework class meant to be subclassed
Languages: Kotlin
class Money(val amount: java.math.BigDecimal, currency: String) {
    var currency: String = currency
        private set
}
open class BaseActivity : Activity()

Key gotchas.

  • The memberwise initializer of a public struct is internal; you must write a public init for other modules to construct it. A frequent error when splitting an app into SPM modules.
  • Extensions in the same file can see private members (Swift 4+), so extension-based code organisation is safe.
  • private(set) is the idiom for a view model's state: readable by the view, writable only by the model.
  • Access cannot be greater than the types it uses (a public function cannot return an internal type).
  • @testable import lets tests see internal symbols.

Real industry examples. Multi-module apps at Airbnb and Spotify (SPM or Bazel modules) rely on public/package boundaries to enforce layering. Swift 6 packages use package to share code between targets without exposing it to clients.

Everyday analogy. private is your bedroom, fileprivate is the whole flat, internal is the building, public lets visitors look but not rearrange the furniture, open lets them rebuild rooms.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming default is public like Kotlin. It is internal.
  • Forgetting a public initializer for a public struct and getting "initializer is inaccessible".
  • Mixing up public and open: only open allows outside subclassing.

notes.title: Swift versus Kotlin syntax cheat sheet
notes.html:
Android equivalent. This is the lookup table to keep open during your first weeks.

Concept Kotlin Swift
Constant / variable val / var let / var
Function fun f(a: Int): Int func f(a: Int) -> Int
Optional String? String? (an enum)
Safe call / elvis ?. / ?: ?. / ??
Force unwrap !! !
String template "$x ${x + 1}" "\(x) \(x + 1)"
Lambda { a -> a + 1 }, it { a in a + 1 }, $0
When when (x) {} switch x {}
Class / data class class / data class class / struct
Singleton object static let shared or an enum with no cases
Interface interface protocol
Extension fun T.f() extension T { func f() }
Companion companion object static members
Enum with payload sealed class enum with associated values
Generics <T : Comparable<T>> <T: Comparable>
Null check + return x ?: return guard let x else { return }
Exceptions throw, try/catch throw, do { try } catch
Coroutines suspend, launch async, Task { }
Scope functions let/apply/also none (use closures or map)
Annotation @Composable attribute @ViewBuilder, @MainActor
Init init / primary ctor init(...), memberwise for structs
Visibility default public internal
Package package x.y module (target)
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct User: Equatable { let id: Int; var name: String }       // data class like
let u = User(id: 1, name: "A")
var v = u; v.name = "B"                                         // copy, like data class copy()
data class User(val id: Int, var name: String)
val u = User(1, "A")
val v = u.copy(name = "B")

Other differences in one glance. No semicolons, no new, no static class for utilities (use a caseless enum or free functions), no top-level main in apps (the @main attribute marks the entry point, e.g. @main struct MyApp: App), strings use \(...), comments // and /* */ (nested comments allowed), print instead of println, nil instead of null, Void is (), and Any (any type) plus AnyObject (any class instance) are the top types.

Everyday analogy. A phrasebook: it will not make you fluent, but it lets you order dinner on day one.

Common interview traps.

  • Searching for static utility classes or object singletons instead of the Swift idioms.
  • Expecting data class features (auto copy): Swift gets Equatable/Hashable synthesis but no built-in copy(...); you copy a struct by assigning it to a var and mutating.
  • Assuming println or it exist.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Baseline: Swift 6, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18, SwiftUI-first, modern APIs; legacy forms are labelled as such.
  • let/var map to val/var; prefer let; let on a struct freezes it entirely.
  • Optionals are a generic enum, not a nullable flag; no smart casts, so you rebind with if let/guard let.
  • guard forces an exit and leaks its bindings into the enclosing scope; use it for preconditions.
  • switch is exhaustive, no fallthrough, and is an expression in Swift 5.9+.
  • Argument labels are part of a function's identity; _ drops one.
  • Closures: trailing closure syntax, $0, non-escaping by default, @escaping when stored, capture lists [weak self] to avoid retain cycles.
  • Strings are grapheme-cluster collections, no integer index, Substring retains its parent.
  • Access control default is internal; open vs public; public structs need a public init.
  • Keep the cheat sheet handy and promote tuples to structs once they spread.
